title: Dropout and generalization
summary: Large networks can memorise their training data. Dropout switches each neuron off with probability p at every training step, so no neuron can rely on particular partners. Inverted dropout divides survivors by 1 − p to keep the expected total; at test time dropout is off. It acts like training a huge family of thinned networks that share weights.
llm_link: The original transformer and the first GPT used dropout with p = 0.1. Some of the largest language models, trained on so much text that they rarely see an example twice, use little or none in pre-training; it stays common when fine-tuning on small datasets.
key_ideas: Overfitting: training error keeps falling while error on new data rises.
Dropout: during training, zero each neuron's output with probability p, with a fresh random mask every step.
Inverted dropout: multiply survivors by 1/(1 − p) so the expected sum is unchanged; at test time use every neuron with no scaling.
Each mask is a thinned network; the full network at test time roughly averages the whole family.
Dropout raises training loss a little but narrows the train/validation gap. Other regularisers: weight decay, early stopping, more data.

quiz.q: Predict the result: inverted dropout with p = 0.5 keeps an activation of 3.0. What value is passed on during training?
quiz.explain: Survivors are divided by the keep probability 1 − p = 0.5, so 3.0 becomes 6.0. The expected value stays 3.0.

quiz.q: What happens to dropout at test time (with inverted dropout)?
options: It uses the same random mask as the last training step
It is switched off: every neuron is used and nothing is rescaled
Every output is multiplied by p
Half the neurons are removed permanently
quiz.explain: Because the rescaling already happened during training, inference simply uses the full network.

options: No neuron can rely on particular partners, so knowledge is spread out, much like averaging many thinned networks
It makes the network smaller at test time
quiz.explain: Random absences break fragile co-adaptations, and the full network behaves roughly like an ensemble average.

quiz.q: With dropout switched on, what usually happens to the training loss compared with no dropout?
quiz.explain: The network always works with a handicap during training, but the gap to validation loss narrows.

quiz.q: Why do some of the largest language models use little or no dropout during pre-training?
options: Dropout does not work with attention
With so much data they rarely see an example twice, so memorisation is less of a threat
Dropout is too slow on GPUs
quiz.explain: Regularisation fights memorisation; with enormous datasets there is less to fight. Fine-tuning on small datasets still often uses it.

problems.title: Inverted dropout by hand
problems.prompt:
Write dropout(x, p, mask) for plain lists. mask is a list of 0s and 1s (1 = keep) that the caller drew at random; your function is deterministic. Kept entries are divided by 1 - p; dropped entries become 0.

dropout([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], 0.5, [1, 0, 1, 0])   # [2.0, 0.0, 6.0, 0.0]

Then write dropout_eval(x), the test-time version: it returns a copy of x unchanged.

tests.name: the example
tests.code:
out = dropout([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], 0.5, [1, 0, 1, 0])
assert out == [2.0, 0.0, 6.0, 0.0], f'kept values are divided by 1 - p = 0.5: expected [2.0, 0.0, 6.0, 0.0], got {out}'

tests.name: p = 0.1 scales by 1/0.9
tests.code:
out = dropout([0.9, 0.9], 0.1, [1, 1])
assert all(abs(v - 1.0) < 1e-9 for v in out), f'0.9 / 0.9 = 1.0, got {out}'

tests.name: expected total is kept
tests.code:
x = [1.0] * 10
mask = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1]
out = dropout(x, 0.1, mask)
assert abs(sum(out) - 10.0) < 1e-9, f'one of ten dropped and the rest scaled by 1/0.9: total should be 10, got {sum(out)}'

tests.name: test time changes nothing
tests.code:
x = [1.0, -2.0, 3.0]
out = dropout_eval(x)
assert out == x, f'at test time the output equals the input, got {out}'
assert out is not x, 'return a new list, not the same object'

hints: [v / (1 - p) if m else 0.0 for v, m in zip(x, mask)]

problems.title: A dropout layer (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Write dropout_layer(X, p, rng, training=True) for an array of any shape. In training mode draw mask = rng.random(X.shape) >= p (True means keep), zero the dropped entries and divide the rest by 1 - p. With training=False return X unchanged.

The tests check the statistics: about a fraction p of entries become zero, and the mean is preserved.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def dropout_layer(X, p, rng, training=True):
    # TODO: if not training, return X
    # TODO: mask = rng.random(X.shape) >= p ; return X * mask / (1 - p)
    return X

tests.name: about p of the entries are zeroed
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.ones((200, 500))
Y = dropout_layer(X, 0.3, np.random.default_rng(0))
frac = (Y == 0).mean()
assert abs(frac - 0.3) < 0.01, f'with p = 0.3 about 30% of entries should be 0, got {frac:.3f}'

tests.name: survivors are scaled up
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.ones((50, 50))
Y = dropout_layer(X, 0.2, np.random.default_rng(1))
kept = Y[Y != 0]
assert np.allclose(kept, 1 / 0.8), f'kept entries should be 1 / (1 - p) = 1.25, got values like {kept[:3]}'

tests.name: the mean is preserved
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.random.default_rng(2).normal(3, 1, size=(300, 300))
Y = dropout_layer(X, 0.5, np.random.default_rng(3))
assert abs(Y.mean() - X.mean()) < 0.05, f'inverted dropout keeps the expected value: input mean {X.mean():.3f}, output mean {Y.mean():.3f}'

tests.name: evaluation mode is the identity
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.arange(12.0).reshape(3, 4)
Y = dropout_layer(X, 0.5, np.random.default_rng(0), training=False)
assert np.array_equal(Y, X), 'with training=False the layer must return X unchanged'

hints:
mask = rng.random(X.shape) >= p
return X * mask / (1 - p)
